title: The Developing Heart and Circulation
summary: How a simple tube loops and divides into a four-chambered heart, and how fetal circulation switches at birth.

lessons.title: Cardiogenic Fields, the Heart Tube and Cardiac Looping

levels.kid:
Your heart is the very first organ that starts working, even before you have arms or a real face! It begins beating about three weeks after a baby starts growing.

At first, the heart is not a heart shape at all. It starts as a flat horseshoe of special cells near the top of the tiny embryo. Then the embryo curls up, and the two sides of the horseshoe come together to make one straight tube, like a drinking straw.

The straw keeps growing longer, but it has no room to stretch. So it bends and twists into an S-shape, a bit like a garden hose crumpling in a small box. This bending puts the parts in the right places, so later they can become four rooms.
levels.hs:
The heart is the **first functional organ** in the embryo. Blood starts moving around day 21 to 22 after fertilization, because a growing embryo is too big to get oxygen by simple diffusion.

Heart cells come from **splanchnic mesoderm**, one layer of the middle germ layer, at the head end of the embryo. Here they form a horseshoe-shaped region called the **cardiac crescent**, or **first heart field**.

Next comes **embryonic folding**. As the flat embryo folds side to side, the two arms of the crescent are brought to the midline and fuse into a single **primitive heart tube**. The tube has layers:
- an inner lining, the **endocardium**
- a thick, jelly-like middle layer, the **cardiac jelly**
- an outer muscle layer, the **myocardium**

From tail to head, the tube has swellings that will become later structures: sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle, bulbus cordis and truncus arteriosus.

Around day 23, the tube starts **cardiac looping**: it bends to the right, forming a **D-loop**. This moves the future ventricles ahead and brings the atria up and behind them.

A real example: in **dextrocardia** with **situs inversus**, the loop and the body organs are mirror-reversed. Many people with this mirror arrangement have normal heart function.
levels.college:
**Origins.** Cardiac progenitors are among the first mesodermal cells to pass through the primitive streak. They migrate to the cranial **lateral plate mesoderm** and settle in its **splanchnic** layer. Signals from the anterior endoderm (BMP2, FGF8) combined with Wnt inhibition (Dkk1, Crescent) induce key cardiac transcription factors: **Nkx2-5**, **GATA4**, **Tbx5** and **MEF2C**.

**Two heart fields.**
- **First heart field (FHF)**: the cardiac crescent. It forms the initial tube and contributes mainly the **left ventricle** and parts of the atria.
- **Second heart field (SHF)**: lies medial and dorsal to the crescent in pharyngeal mesoderm. It is marked by **Isl1** and **Tbx1**. It adds cells to both poles of the tube. At the arterial pole it builds the **right ventricle** and **outflow tract**; at the venous pole it adds atrial tissue.

**Tube formation.** Lateral folding brings the paired endocardial tubes together, and they fuse at the midline. Head folding swings the heart region beneath the foregut into the future thorax, ventral to it. The tube hangs in the pericardial cavity from the **dorsal mesocardium**, which later breaks down to form the **transverse pericardial sinus**. Peristaltic contractions begin around day 22.

**Looping (days 23 to 28).** The tube bends ventrally and to the right (**D-looping**). As a result:
- the bulbus cordis lies to the right
- the primitive ventricle lies to the left
- the atria move dorsal and cranial

Looping lines up the inflow and outflow regions so they can later be divided by septa.

**Left-right cues.** Nodal flow at the primitive node triggers **Nodal**, **Lefty** and **Pitx2c** on the left side. These signals set the direction of the loop. Defects in this pathway cause **heterotaxy** and abnormal looping.
levels.phd:
**Lineage architecture.** Clonal analysis by Meilhac and Buckingham, using retrospective lineage tracing with the laacZ method in mouse, showed two lineages that separate early. The first lineage, the FHF, contributes to the left ventricle. The second lineage, the SHF, contributes to the outflow tract and right ventricle, and both lineages contribute to the atria. Both share a common Mesp1-positive progenitor. Mesp1 is transiently expressed in nascent mesoderm, and its descendants include almost all myocardium.

The SHF has subdomains:
- an **anterior SHF**, marked by Fgf10 and an Mef2c-AHF enhancer
- a **posterior SHF**, which gives the inflow region

The SHF stays proliferative and undifferentiated because of FGF8/10 and Wnt/β-catenin signaling, together with Tbx1 and Hedgehog. It differentiates as it is added to the tube under BMP influence. Islet1 was first described as an SHF marker (Cai et al., 2003). Later work showed Isl1 is also expressed transiently in FHF progenitors, so a strict marker-based division is debated.

**Tube elongation.** Tube growth is driven largely by **addition of cells at the poles**, not by expansion of a fixed cell population. DiI labeling in chick (de la Cruz; Kelly) showed that the early linear tube consists mostly of future left ventricle. The **chamber formation model** (Christoffels and Moorman) holds that working chamber myocardium balloons out from the outer curvature of the looped tube. These ballooning regions express Nppa and Cx40. The inner curvature and AV canal stay primitive, repressed by Tbx2 and Tbx3, which are induced by BMP2.

**Looping mechanics.** Looping is partly intrinsic: isolated chick tubes still bend. Bending comes from differences in cell shape, orientation and proliferation. Torsion also comes from extrinsic forces such as the splanchnopleure, and from intrinsic cytoskeletal chirality. Pitx2c tells the SHF and dorsal mesocardium about left-right identity. Le Garrec et al. (2017) proposed that rightward rotation arises from asymmetric cell ingression at the poles, and that the tube buckles because it is fixed at both ends.
levels.expert:
**Clinical genetics of early cardiogenesis.** Mutations in the core transcription factors cause congenital heart disease, often with a clear phenotype for each gene:
- **NKX2-5**: secundum atrial septal defect with progressive AV block
- **TBX5**: Holt-Oram syndrome, with ASD/VSD and radial ray defects
- **GATA4**: septal defects
- **TBX1**: haploinsufficiency within the 22q11.2 deletion, which disrupts the SHF and the outflow tract

The SHF framework explains why conotruncal anomalies cluster with pharyngeal and craniofacial defects. Those defects themselves belong to later lessons.

**Laterality disorders.** **Heterotaxy** (isomerism) arises from failed Nodal/Pitx2 signaling. Genes involved include ZIC3, CFC1, NODAL and the ciliary genes. In **primary ciliary dyskinesia**, nodal cilia do not beat properly, so left-right asymmetry is randomized. About half of patients have situs inversus totalis, often with normal heart function. Situs ambiguus carries much higher rates of complex heart disease. The direction of the loop can also be uncoupled from visceral situs. An **L-loop** places the morphologic right ventricle on the left, as seen in congenitally corrected transposition.

**Teratologic sensitivity.** The heart's critical window runs roughly from weeks 3 to 8. Exposures during field specification and looping have cardiac consequences:
- **Retinoic acid excess**: retinoic acid patterns the posterior SHF and inflow tract, which explains isotretinoin embryopathy
- **Maternal hyperglycemia**: in pregestational diabetes, looping and outflow tract defects increase

**Research frontiers.**
- **Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics** have mapped mouse and human cardiac progenitors and uncovered further populations. One example is a juxta-cardiac field that contributes to the epicardium and to early myocardium (Tyser et al., 2021).
- **Cardiac organoids** ("cardioids", Hofbauer et al., 2021) self-organize into chambers. They model FHF identity and allow live study of early morphogenesis.
- **Light-sheet imaging and biomechanical modeling** now measure looping forces in vivo.

Open questions remain:
- Do the FHF and SHF truly represent separate lineages, or a spatiotemporal continuum?
- How do the inherent chiral properties of cells combine with Nodal cues?
- Why do people with identical variants show such variable phenotypes, which points to modifier and environmental effects?

keyPoints: The heart is the first functional organ; it beats from about day 22
Heart cells arise from splanchnic mesoderm in the cardiac crescent
First heart field makes the left ventricle; second heart field adds the right ventricle and outflow tract
Folding fuses paired tubes into one heart tube: endocardium, cardiac jelly, myocardium
The tube D-loops to the right, setting up future chambers
Nodal, Lefty and Pitx2 on the left set looping direction; defects cause heterotaxy

test.q: Which embryonic tissue gives rise to heart muscle cells?
test.explain: Cardiac progenitors settle in the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm. Somatic mesoderm forms the body wall instead.

test.q: Around when does the embryonic heart begin to beat?
test.explain: Contractions start around day 21-22, making the heart the first functional organ.

test.q: The first heart field contributes mainly to which structure?
test.explain: The FHF (cardiac crescent) forms the early tube, mostly future left ventricle. The second heart field builds the right ventricle and outflow tract.

test.q: What is the gelatinous layer between endocardium and myocardium?
test.explain: Cardiac jelly lies between the inner endocardium and outer myocardium of the primitive tube.

test.q: In normal looping, the heart tube bends toward the:
test.explain: Normal looping is rightward, called D-looping.

test.q: What brings the two sides of the cardiac crescent to the midline?
choices: Outgrowth of the upper limb buds
test.explain: Lateral folding of the embryo brings the paired endocardial tubes together to fuse.

test.q: Which marker is classically associated with the second heart field?
test.explain: Islet1 (Isl1) marks second heart field progenitors, along with Tbx1.

test.q: Mirror-image reversal of the heart together with all body organs is called:
test.explain: Situs inversus is a full mirror reversal, often with normal heart function. Heterotaxy is a disordered, non-mirror arrangement.

test.q: Which gene is expressed on the left side and helps set looping direction?
test.explain: Pitx2 (with Nodal and Lefty) carries left-sided identity. Nkx2-5 is a general cardiac factor, not a laterality signal.

test.q: The horseshoe-shaped region of first heart cells is the cardiac ___.
test.explain: The cardiac crescent is the first heart field.

test.q: What is the inner endothelial lining of the heart tube called?
test.explain: The endocardium lines the tube; the myocardium forms the outer muscle.

test.q: Breakdown of the dorsal mesocardium forms the transverse pericardial ___.
test.explain: The transverse pericardial sinus forms when the dorsal mesocardium breaks down.

kidTest.q: Which organ starts working first in a baby?
kidTest.explain: The heart beats very early, about three weeks after a baby starts growing.

kidTest.q: What shape do the first heart cells make?
kidTest.explain: They start as a flat horseshoe shape.

kidTest.q: What does the heart look like after the sides join?
kidTest.explain: The two sides come together into one tube, like a straw.

kidTest.q: Why does the heart tube bend and twist?
choices: It gets pushed by the arms
kidTest.explain: It grows longer in a small space, so it bends into an S-shape.

kidTest.q: The early heart looks like a drinking s _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The heart tube is straight like a drinking straw before it bends.

advancedTest.q: If second heart field cells failed to be added to the arterial pole, which defect would you predict?
choices: Absence of the sinus venosus with normal ventricles
A small left ventricle with a normal outflow tract
Mirror reversal of the thoracic and abdominal organs
A short outflow tract and an underdeveloped right ventricle
advancedTest.explain: The SHF adds the outflow tract and right ventricle at the arterial pole. The left ventricle comes mainly from the FHF.

advancedTest.q: Why do isolated chick heart tubes still bend, and what does this imply?
choices: Nodal signaling is reactivated within the cultured tube
Blood pressure inside them persists, so flow drives looping
Ventricular chambers balloon first and then pull the tube
Looping has an intrinsic tissue component beyond outside forces
advancedTest.explain: Bending without the surrounding embryo shows that cell shape and growth differences within the tube contribute. Extrinsic forces add to this.

advancedTest.q: Ciliary dyskinesia producing situs inversus in about half of patients best supports which model?
choices: Cilia directly contract to bend the heart tube rightward
Nodal flow biases sidedness; without it, laterality is random
Pitx2 is expressed on both sides when cilia beat normally
Left-right sidedness depends on maternal hormone gradients
advancedTest.explain: Immotile nodal cilia remove the directional bias, so situs is randomized and about half of patients end up reversed.

advancedTest.q: Under the chamber formation model, why does the AV canal stay non-ballooning myocardium?
choices: Nppa and Cx40 are strongly induced in the canal
Retinoic acid excess blocks myocardium in the canal
BMP2-induced Tbx2 and Tbx3 repress chamber genes there
Second heart field cells there remain undifferentiated
advancedTest.explain: Tbx2 and Tbx3 repress the chamber program in the AV canal. Nppa and Cx40 mark the ballooning chambers instead.

lessons.title: Septation of the Atria and Atrioventricular Canal

levels.kid:
Early on, a baby's heart is like one big room. To work well, it needs walls to split it into separate rooms.

First, a thin curtain grows down from the ceiling of the top room. Then a thicker wall grows next to it. But the builder leaves a little doorway between them on purpose! This doorway is called the **foramen ovale**. Before birth, the baby gets oxygen from mom, not from its lungs, so blood can slip through this door.

At the same time, soft pillows called **cushions** grow in the middle of the heart. They meet and divide the opening into a left door and a right door. Later these doors get little flaps called **valves**.

After birth, the doorway between the top rooms closes like a door clicking shut.
levels.hs:
After the heart tube loops, it has one shared **atrium** (upper chamber) connected to one ventricle region through a single opening, the **atrioventricular (AV) canal**. Around weeks 4 to 6 of development, walls called **septa** divide these spaces.

Dividing the atria:
- A thin, crescent-shaped wall, the **septum primum**, grows down from the roof of the atrium. The gap below its edge is the **ostium primum**.
- Before the ostium primum closes, holes open in the upper part of the septum primum and merge into the **ostium secundum**.
- A thicker wall, the **septum secundum**, grows just to the right of the first one. It leaves an oval gap, the **foramen ovale**.

The two septa overlap like a one-way flap valve. In the fetus, blood pressure is higher in the right atrium, so blood flows right to left, skipping the lungs, which are not yet used for breathing. At birth, left-sided pressure rises, the flap is pushed shut, and the two septa usually fuse.

Dividing the AV canal: swellings of tissue called **endocardial cushions** grow from the top and bottom of the canal and fuse, splitting it into right and left openings. These later get the **tricuspid** and **mitral valves**.

A real example: in about 25% of adults the flap never fully seals, a harmless-sounding gap called a **patent foramen ovale (PFO)**.
levels.college:
Atrial and AV septation proceed together from roughly day 26 to day 42 (weeks 4 to 6), turning the looped tube's common atrium and single AV canal into two atria and two AV orifices.

**Atrial septum**
- **Septum primum** grows from the atrial roof toward the AV canal. It carries a **mesenchymal cap** on its leading edge.
- The **ostium primum** narrows as the septum advances. It closes when the cap fuses with the endocardial cushions, aided by the **dorsal mesenchymal protrusion (DMP)**, tissue from the second heart field that enters through the dorsal mesocardium.
- Before closure, **programmed cell death** perforates the upper septum primum, creating the **ostium secundum**. This keeps right-to-left flow going.
- The muscular **septum secundum** forms to the right, as an infolding of the atrial roof. Its free edge bounds the **foramen ovale**. The septum primum flap becomes the **valve of the foramen ovale**, and its remnant later forms the floor of the **fossa ovalis**.

**AV canal**
- The superior and inferior **endocardial cushions** fuse in the midline, giving right and left AV canals. Lateral cushions contribute to valve leaflets.
- Cushions arise by **endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)**: endocardial cells, signaled by myocardium through **BMP2** and **TGF-beta**, invade the **cardiac jelly**.
- The AV canal also shifts rightward so that both atria line up over their ventricles.
- **Mitral** (bicuspid) and **tricuspid** leaflets are sculpted from cushion tissue. Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles form from the remodeled ventricular wall.

**Defects**
- **Secundum ASD**: most common type, from excess resorption of septum primum or a small septum secundum.
- **Primum ASD and atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD)**: failed cushion fusion, often with a cleft mitral valve. These are strongly associated with **trisomy 21**.
- **PFO**: failed postnatal fusion of the two septa.
levels.phd:
**Cushion EMT.** AV cushion formation is a model of developmental EMT. Myocardial **BMP2** induces **Twist1** and **Snail/Slug** in overlying endocardium. **Notch1** signaling (Delta-like4/Jagged1 to RBPJ) drives Snail, which represses **VE-cadherin**, letting cells delaminate. **TGF-beta2/3** and **ErbB** signaling, through **neuregulin** and **hyaluronan** (made by **Has2**), support invasion and swelling of the cardiac jelly. Restriction of cushions to the AV canal and outflow tract depends on **Tbx2/Tbx3**, which suppress chamber genes such as **Nppa** in AV myocardium. Chick explant assays on collagen gels (Runyan and Markwald) established that myocardium supplies the inductive signal.

**Second heart field contribution.** The classic view had the septum primum growing down alone to fuse with the cushions. Lineage tracing (Isl1-Cre, among others) and work by Snarr and colleagues showed that the **DMP**, an Isl1+ and Tbx5-dependent posterior SHF population, is essential. **Hedgehog** signaling through Gli is needed for DMP growth, and SHF-specific Smo deletion produces primum ASD and AVSD. This reframed AVSD as partly a defect of second heart field morphogenesis, not purely of the cushions.

**Transcriptional network.** **NKX2-5**, **GATA4** and **TBX5** interact physically and genetically. Heterozygous NKX2-5 mutations (Schott et al., 1998) cause secundum ASD with progressive AV conduction block. TBX5 haploinsufficiency causes **Holt-Oram syndrome**, which combines ASD with upper-limb defects. GATA4 G296S disrupts its interaction with TBX5. Dosage sensitivity is a recurring theme.

**Trisomy 21.** About 40 to 50% of Down syndrome infants have congenital heart disease, and AVSD is the signature lesion. Candidate genes include **COL6A1/2**, **DSCAM** and **RCAN1** (a calcineurin/NFAT modulator). Since NFATc1 is required for valve remodeling, RCAN1 links chromosome 21 dosage to cushion biology. Penetrance is incomplete, so second-hit modifiers such as **CRELD1** variants are invoked. Exactly which genes are responsible is still debated.

**Fetal shunt physiology.** The foramen ovale's flap-valve geometry preferentially directs oxygen-rich inferior caval blood, steered by the **Eustachian valve**, into the left atrium.
levels.expert:
**Clinical classification maps onto embryology.** Interatrial communications include secundum ASD (about 75%), primum ASD (a partial AVSD), **sinus venosus** defects (superior or inferior, often with anomalous right pulmonary venous return), and the **unroofed coronary sinus**. Strictly, sinus venosus and coronary sinus defects lie outside the true septum, since they come from venous pole remodeling rather than failure of the primum/secundum overlap. Recognizing this matters: catheter devices suit only secundum defects with adequate rims, typically meaning a deficient aortic rim is tolerable but deficient IVC or posterior rims are not. Primum and sinus venosus defects need surgery.

**AVSD spectrum.** **Partial** AVSD has a primum ASD plus a cleft left AV valve and two separate valve orifices. **Complete** AVSD has a common AV valve and an inlet VSD. The **Rastelli classification** (types A to C) grades the anatomy of the superior bridging leaflet. Repair is usually done in infancy, and a recurrent pitfall is left AV valve regurgitation. Because the AV node is displaced posteroinferiorly and the conduction axis runs along the deficient inlet septum, suture placement risks **heart block**. This embryologic displacement is something surgeons must account for.

**PFO in neurology.** For a neurosurgery-minded reader, the PFO is the key lesson. **Paradoxical embolism** across a PFO is implicated in cryptogenic stroke in younger patients. The CLOSE, RESPECT and REDUCE trials (2017) showed that device closure lowers recurrent stroke compared with medical therapy in selected patients aged 18 to 60. The **RoPE score** and the **PASCAL** classification estimate whether a PFO is likely causal. Large shunts and an **atrial septal aneurysm** raise risk. Atrial fibrillation after closure is a known trade-off. In neurosurgery, a PFO matters in **sitting-position** posterior fossa surgery, because venous air embolism can cross and become arterial. Preoperative bubble echocardiography is often performed.

**Genetics in practice.** Familial ASD with PR prolongation should prompt **NKX2-5** testing and ongoing conduction surveillance, since block can progress after repair.

**Open questions.** How DMP and cushion tissues are coordinated mechanically is still unclear. The role of flow (hemodynamic shear sensed through **KLF2** and primary cilia) in valve maturation is being worked out. Human iPSC-derived and organoid models of cushion EMT are emerging but do not yet reproduce septal three-dimensional geometry.

keyPoints: Septum primum grows down; ostium secundum opens by cell death before ostium primum closes
Septum secundum leaves the foramen ovale, a flap valve that allows fetal right-to-left flow
Endocardial cushions, formed by EMT, fuse to split the AV canal and build the AV valves
The second heart field's dorsal mesenchymal protrusion helps close the ostium primum
NKX2-5, GATA4 and TBX5 mutations cause ASDs; trisomy 21 is linked to AVSD
Patent foramen ovale (~25% of adults) enables paradoxical embolism and stroke

test.q: Which structure grows first from the roof of the common atrium?
test.explain: The thin septum primum appears first. The septum secundum forms later, to its right.

test.q: How does the ostium secundum form?
choices: Folding of the atrial roof inward
Programmed cell death in the septum
test.explain: Perforations caused by cell death in the upper septum primum merge to form the ostium secundum before the ostium primum closes.

test.q: Why does blood cross the foramen ovale from right to left before birth?
choices: The ventricles pump blood back upward
Lung vessels have very low resistance
Right atrial pressure is higher than left
The mitral valve stays closed in the fetus
test.explain: Fetal right atrial pressure exceeds left atrial pressure, so the septum primum flap opens to the left. Fetal lung resistance is high, not low.

test.q: What closes the foramen ovale functionally at birth?
test.explain: When breathing begins, pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and pushes the flap against the septum secundum.

test.q: Endocardial cushions mainly divide which space?
test.explain: The superior and inferior AV cushions fuse to split the single AV canal into right and left openings.

test.q: Cushion cells arise from endocardium through which process?
test.explain: Endocardial cells undergo EMT, signaled by myocardial BMP2 and TGF-beta, and invade the cardiac jelly.

test.q: Which is the most common type of atrial septal defect?
test.explain: Secundum ASDs make up about 75% of cases and result from too much septum primum resorption or a small septum secundum.

test.q: Atrioventricular septal defects are strongly associated with:
test.explain: AVSD is the signature heart defect of Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

test.q: The dorsal mesenchymal protrusion comes from which source?
test.explain: The DMP is Isl1+ second heart field tissue that enters through the dorsal mesocardium and helps close the ostium primum.

test.q: The oval gap left by the septum secundum is the foramen ___.
test.explain: The foramen ovale is the fetal shunt between the atria.

test.q: What AV valve forms on the left side from cushion tissue?
test.explain: The left AV valve is the mitral (bicuspid) valve. The right one is the tricuspid.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for an unsealed foramen ovale in adults?
test.explain: A patent foramen ovale is present in about 25% of adults.

kidTest.q: What does an early baby heart need to grow?
choices: Bones to make it strong and hard
Hair to keep it warm and safe
kidTest.explain: Walls split the heart into separate rooms.

kidTest.q: Why can blood pass through the doorway before birth?
choices: The baby's heart is very cold
The baby gets oxygen from mom
kidTest.explain: The lungs are not used yet, so blood can skip them.

kidTest.q: What do the soft cushions in the heart do?
choices: They make left and right doors
kidTest.explain: The cushions meet and split the opening into two doors.

kidTest.q: What happens to the doorway after birth?
kidTest.explain: After birth, the doorway between the top rooms shuts.

kidTest.q: Little flaps on the heart doors are called v _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Valves are flaps that keep blood moving the right way.

advancedTest.q: SHF-specific Smo deletion produces primum ASD and AVSD. This best supports which conclusion?
choices: Programmed cell death in septum primum is controlled by Smo
Septum secundum growth depends on neural crest Hedgehog signals
Hedgehog-driven DMP growth is needed to close the ostium primum
Cushion EMT is driven by Hedgehog acting on the endocardium
advancedTest.explain: Hedgehog acts on second heart field cells that form the DMP. Without it, the ostium primum stays open, which recasts AVSD as partly an SHF defect.

advancedTest.q: A family has secundum ASDs plus a progressively longer PR interval. Which gene is the most likely cause?
advancedTest.explain: NKX2-5 mutations cause ASD with progressive AV conduction block. TBX5 would also cause limb defects (Holt-Oram syndrome).

advancedTest.q: Why is a sinus venosus defect not suitable for catheter device closure, unlike many secundum ASDs?
choices: It arises outside the true atrial septum
It is caused by a failure of AV cushion fusion
It tends to close on its own by early childhood
It usually shunts blood from right to left instead
advancedTest.explain: Sinus venosus defects come from venous pole remodeling, so they lie outside the true septum, lack the rims a device needs, and often come with anomalous pulmonary venous return, so they need surgery.

advancedTest.q: During complete AVSD repair, suture placement along the inlet septum mainly risks:
advancedTest.explain: The AV node is displaced posteroinferiorly and the conduction axis runs along the deficient inlet septum, so sutures there can cause heart block.

lessons.title: Outflow Tract and Ventricular Septation

levels.kid:
Your heart has two big pipes leaving it. One pipe sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The other pipe sends blood to your whole body.

But in a tiny growing baby, these two pipes start as just one tube! Then two soft ridges grow inside the tube. They twist around each other like a candy cane stripe and meet in the middle. Now there are two pipes instead of one.

The bottom part of the heart also gets a wall down the middle. This wall keeps the blood going to the lungs apart from the blood going to the body.

If the wall has a hole, or the pipes don't twist right, a baby can be born with a heart problem. Heart doctors can often fix it.
levels.hs:
Early in development the heart has a single exit tube called the **outflow tract** (the conotruncus and truncus arteriosus). In the finished heart that one tube has become two great arteries: the **aorta**, carrying blood from the left ventricle to the body, and the **pulmonary trunk**, carrying blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

The split happens during weeks 5 to 8:
- Swellings called **outflow tract cushions** (truncoconal ridges) grow inside the tube.
- They spiral about 180 degrees and fuse, forming the **aorticopulmonary septum**. Because the septum spirals, the aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other.
- Special cells called **neural crest cells** travel from the developing brain region and help build this septum.

Meanwhile, the single ventricle is divided by the **interventricular septum**. A thick **muscular** part grows up from the floor of the heart. A thin **membranous** part closes the last gap near the top.

The most common heart defect at birth is a **ventricular septal defect (VSD)**, a hole in this wall. Most VSDs sit in the membranous part. If the septum doesn't spiral, the arteries can end up attached to the wrong ventricles. This is called **transposition of the great arteries**, and babies with it need surgery soon after birth.
levels.college:
**The outflow tract (OFT)** is added largely by the **second heart field (SHF)** at the arterial pole and divides into a proximal **conus** (bulbus cordis) and a distal **truncus arteriosus**. Septation runs from distal to proximal:
- **Aortic sac/distal truncus**: a dorsal **aortopulmonary septum** (from SHF mesenchyme plus neural crest) separates the 4th and 6th arch arteries.
- **Truncal and conal cushions**: endocardial cushion tissue, filled with **cardiac neural crest cells** coming from the rhombencephalon via pharyngeal arches 3, 4 and 6, forms opposing ridges. The ridges fuse in a **spiral**, producing the aorticopulmonary septum. This explains why the pulmonary trunk wraps anterior to and around the aorta.
- The conal cushions **myocardialize**, becoming the muscular outlet septum and the subpulmonary **infundibulum**.
- Smaller intercalated cushions form the **semilunar valve** leaflets.

**Ventricular septation:**
- The **muscular interventricular septum** forms from apposition of the expanding ("ballooning") left and right ventricular walls, leaving an **interventricular foramen**.
- That foramen closes around week 7 to 8 by fusion of conal cushion tissue, AV cushion tissue (inferior cushion) and the muscular septum. The result is the **membranous septum**.
- The aorta must shift ("wedge") over the left ventricle, aligning the left ventricle with the aorta.

**Classic defects:**
- **Membranous (perimembranous) VSD**: the most common form.
- **Persistent truncus arteriosus**: no septation, so one vessel overrides a VSD. Linked to neural crest deficiency.
- **Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)**: the septum fails to spiral.
- **Tetralogy of Fallot**: anterosuperior deviation of the outlet septum causes pulmonary stenosis, an overriding aorta, VSD and right ventricular hypertrophy.
- **Double-outlet right ventricle (DORV)**: both arteries arise mainly from the right ventricle.
levels.phd:
OFT development integrates three lineages: **SHF progenitors** (Isl1+, Tbx1-, Fgf8-, Fgf10-dependent) that lengthen the tube and give rise to OFT myocardium and smooth muscle at the arterial pole; **endocardium**, which undergoes **endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT)** to form cushion mesenchyme; and **cardiac neural crest (CNC)**.

EndMT is driven by myocardial **BMP2/4**, endocardial **Notch** (Notch1, Jag1), TGF-beta and Snail/Slug, with cushion expansion supported by hyaluronan (Has2) and Sox9.

Kirby's quail-chick ablation experiments in the 1980s showed that removing premigratory CNC causes **persistent truncus arteriosus**, establishing the neural crest's essential role. CNC cells condense into the septal prongs, signal via **Semaphorin3C/PlexinA2** and endothelin-1/EdnrA, and later undergo apoptosis. They contribute smooth muscle to the arch arteries rather than to myocardium.

CNC failure also secondarily impairs SHF addition. This leaves a shortened OFT with misalignment, a two-way interaction between the lineages. Overall, alignment defects reflect an OFT that is too short or rotates incorrectly.

Regionalized SHF populations matter here:
- **Tbx1** (deleted in **22q11.2 deletion syndrome**) promotes SHF proliferation via Fgf8/10. Its loss shortens the OFT and causes truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot or interrupted aortic arch type B.
- Subpulmonary myocardium derives preferentially from a distinct SHF subdomain. Its deficiency underlies right ventricular outflow hypoplasia in tetralogy of Fallot.
- Bajolle and colleagues proposed that **OFT rotation** (a counterclockwise twist of the myocardium) positions the arteries. Failed rotation contributes to transposition and double-outlet right ventricle.
- Pitx2c-dependent left-right asymmetry influences this rotation.

The muscular septum arises from ballooning compact/trabecular myocardium (marked by Hand1/Hand2 domains and Tbx5 with a sharp boundary). **Tbx5** misexpression shifts septal position, and its loss causes VSDs in Holt-Oram syndrome. **Nkx2-5** and **Gata4** mutations cause familial septal defects.

The classic "spiral septum" model is debated. Many researchers now emphasize opposing cushions plus myocardial rotation rather than a literally helical ridge.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the language of outflow tract and ventricular septal defects maps onto embryology through **segmental analysis**. Clinicians describe atrial situs, atrioventricular connections and **ventriculoarterial connections** in sequence. Alignment defects (TGA, DORV, tetralogy of Fallot) differ in degree along a spectrum of OFT malrotation and outlet septal deviation. For this reason, the Anderson/Van Praagh debates over defining DORV (the "50% rule" versus fibrous continuity) still affect surgical planning.

VSD classification (perimembranous, muscular, inlet, doubly committed juxta-arterial) matters surgically:
- The **conduction system** (the His bundle) runs along the posteroinferior rim of perimembranous defects. Sutures there risk complete heart block.
- Doubly committed defects lack the outlet septum and can lead to aortic cusp prolapse.
- Many small muscular VSDs close spontaneously.
- Large defects cause excess pulmonary blood flow. If left uncorrected, this can lead to Eisenmenger physiology.

Two key surgical repairs:
- **Arterial switch** (Jatene) for d-TGA moves the arteries and coronaries back to the correct ventricles. Before surgery, newborns depend on mixing between the circulations, so prostaglandin E1 and balloon atrial septostomy are used to keep blood mixing.
- **Tetralogy of Fallot** repair closes the VSD and relieves right ventricular outflow obstruction. Pulmonary regurgitation later in life is common and often requires valve replacement, increasingly done by transcatheter techniques.

Genetic workup is standard for conotruncal lesions. 22q11.2 deletion is found in a large share of patients with interrupted aortic arch type B and truncus arteriosus, and a meaningful minority with tetralogy of Fallot. This deletion carries risks of hypocalcemia, immunodeficiency and later psychiatric illness. These conditions should be anticipated, including careful handling of blood products in suspected immunodeficiency.

For neurologically minded trainees, there is an important link between the heart and brain. Neonates with TGA or hypoplastic physiology show delayed brain maturation and periventricular white matter injury even before surgery. This is attributed to reduced cerebral oxygen delivery in utero, and fetal MRI studies document smaller brain volumes. Neurodevelopmental outcome is now a primary endpoint in congenital heart surgery.

Open questions remain:
- How the second heart field and neural crest coordinate their signaling.
- Whether fetal intervention could change outcomes.
- How maternal diabetes and retinoic acid excess disrupt conotruncal development.

keyPoints: The single outflow tract divides into the aorta and pulmonary trunk
Fused, spiraling cushions form the aorticopulmonary septum
Cardiac neural crest cells are essential for outflow septation
Muscular septum grows from the floor; membranous septum closes the foramen
Perimembranous VSD is the most common congenital heart defect
Truncus arteriosus, TGA and tetralogy of Fallot are conotruncal defects

test.q: The embryonic outflow tract normally divides into which two vessels?
test.explain: Septation of the conotruncus creates the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

test.q: Which migrating cell population is essential for building the aorticopulmonary septum?
test.explain: Neural crest from the hindbrain region populates the outflow cushions. Ablating it causes persistent truncus arteriosus.

test.q: Why do the aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other?
choices: The septum forms in a spiral
test.explain: The outflow ridges fuse in a spiral (with myocardial rotation), leaving the great arteries intertwined.

test.q: Where are most ventricular septal defects located?
test.explain: Perimembranous VSDs are the most common type, because closure of the membranous part is the last and most complex step.

test.q: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral results in:
choices: Atrial septal defect of the secundum type
Coarctation of the descending thoracic aorta
Tetralogy of Fallot with an overriding aorta
test.explain: A straight septum connects the aorta to the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk to the left ventricle.

test.q: Persistent truncus arteriosus is most directly caused by:
test.explain: With no septum, one vessel leaves both ventricles over a VSD. It is linked to neural crest deficiency.

test.q: Which feature is NOT part of tetralogy of Fallot?
test.explain: The tetralogy is pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD and right ventricular hypertrophy. An atrial septal defect is not one of the four.

test.q: The membranous ventricular septum is formed by fusion of the muscular septum with tissue from:
test.explain: Conal (outflow) cushion and inferior AV cushion tissue close the interventricular foramen.

test.q: Which heart field lengthens the outflow tract at the arterial pole?
test.explain: Second heart field progenitors are added to the arterial pole and build outflow myocardium.

test.q: The opening between the ventricles that closes around week 7 is the interventricular ___.
test.explain: The interventricular foramen is sealed by the membranous septum.

test.q: What abbreviation describes a hole in the wall between the ventricles?
test.explain: VSD stands for ventricular septal defect.

test.q: The chromosomal syndrome that removes Tbx1 and is linked to conotruncal defects is 22q11.2 ___ syndrome.
test.explain: 22q11.2 deletion removes Tbx1, which impairs second heart field growth.

kidTest.q: How many big pipes leave a grown heart?
kidTest.explain: One pipe goes to the lungs and one goes to the body.

kidTest.q: What does a tiny baby's heart start with?
kidTest.explain: There is one tube at first, which later splits into two.

kidTest.q: What grows inside the tube to split it?
kidTest.explain: Two ridges twist and meet to make two pipes.

kidTest.q: Where does one big pipe send blood?
kidTest.explain: One pipe takes blood to the lungs for oxygen.

kidTest.q: The bottom part of the heart gets a w _ _ _ down the middle.
kidTest.explain: The wall keeps lung blood and body blood apart.

advancedTest.q: Ablating cardiac neural crest leads to a short, misaligned outflow tract. The best explanation is that:
choices: Neural crest directly forms the bulk of ventricular myocardium
The ablation also removes the first heart field progenitor cells
Its loss secondarily reduces second heart field addition
Neural crest controls closure of the atrial septum in the embryo
advancedTest.explain: Neural crest and second heart field interact. Neural crest failure reduces SHF addition, shortening the tract, even though neural crest contributes no myocardium.

advancedTest.q: A Tbx1-null embryo most likely shows which phenotype?
choices: Persistent truncus arteriosus from reduced SHF growth
Isolated apical muscular VSD with normal arteries
Atrial septal defect from failed septum primum
Holt-Oram limb and septal anomalies from Tbx5 loss
advancedTest.explain: Tbx1 drives SHF proliferation via Fgf8/10. Its loss shortens the outflow tract and blocks septation.

advancedTest.q: Why does repairing a perimembranous VSD carry a particular risk of heart block?
choices: The His bundle runs along the posteroinferior rim
Coronary arteries cross the membranous region
The sinus node is in the outlet septum
The AV node lies in the muscular apex
advancedTest.explain: The conducting His bundle runs near the posteroinferior margin of perimembranous defects, so sutures placed there can injure it.

advancedTest.q: TGA, DORV and tetralogy of Fallot are best grouped as:
choices: Defects caused mainly by atrial looping errors
A spectrum of outflow rotation and alignment errors
Defects of venous return to the atria
Disorders of semilunar valve leaflet formation
advancedTest.explain: All three reflect ventriculoarterial misalignment from abnormal outflow tract rotation, length or outlet septum deviation.

lessons.title: Aortic Arches and Venous System Remodeling

levels.kid:
Imagine a brand-new town with lots of small roads. As the town grows, some roads become big highways, and others are closed because nobody needs them. A baby's blood vessels grow the same way!

Early on, the tiny baby has matching pipes on the left and the right, like a ladder. Over time, the body keeps some pipes, makes some bigger, and lets others shrink away. One pipe becomes the big **aorta**, the main road for blood leaving the heart. Others become the roads to the head and arms.

Veins change too. Many veins start on both sides. Later, most of the blood is sent to the right side, so it can flow straight back into the heart.
levels.hs:
In the early embryo, blood leaves the heart through a tube called the **aortic sac**. From there, paired vessels called **pharyngeal arch arteries** (often still called aortic arches) loop around the throat region. They join two **dorsal aortae** that run down the back. There are five pairs, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Pair 5 either never forms or disappears almost immediately.

The arches never all exist at the same time. Arches 1 and 2 mostly disappear early. Then:
- **Arch 3** becomes the common carotid and the start of the internal carotid arteries, which supply the brain.
- **Left arch 4** becomes part of the **arch of the aorta**. **Right arch 4** becomes the start of the right subclavian artery.
- **Arch 6** becomes the pulmonary arteries. On the left it also forms the **ductus arteriosus**, a fetal shortcut that lets blood skip the lungs.

The veins also start out symmetrical. Three pairs drain into the heart: **vitelline** veins from the yolk sac, **umbilical** veins from the placenta, and **cardinal** veins from the body. Over time, blood is shifted to the right side. This is how a single **superior vena cava** and a single **inferior vena cava** form.

A real example: the **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** hooks under the ductus arteriosus. That is why it loops down into the chest before climbing back up to the larynx.
levels.college:
**Arterial system.** The heart's outflow (truncus arteriosus) opens into the **aortic sac**. This sac sends a series of **pharyngeal arch arteries** through each arch to paired **dorsal aortae**. The two dorsal aortae fuse below about the T4 level into a single descending aorta. The arch arteries appear one after another between roughly weeks 4 and 6, and they are rebuilt as they appear:
- **1st**: mostly regresses; leaves part of the maxillary artery.
- **2nd**: mostly regresses; leaves the hyoid and stapedial arteries.
- **3rd**: common carotid and the proximal internal carotid. The external carotid sprouts from it.
- **4th**: on the left, the aortic arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian. On the right, the proximal right subclavian artery.
- **6th**: the proximal pulmonary arteries. The distal left 6th becomes the **ductus arteriosus**. The distal right 6th regresses.

Other key events:
- The **right dorsal aorta** regresses between the origin of the 7th intersegmental artery and the point where the two aortae fuse.
- The aortic sac forms the brachiocephalic trunk and the proximal aortic arch.
- The **7th intersegmental arteries** form the left subclavian and the distal right subclavian.
- The carotid segments lengthen as the heart moves down into the chest.

**Recurrent laryngeal nerves.** These nerves come off the vagus nerve and hook under the 6th arches. On the right, the distal 6th and 5th arches disappear, so the nerve moves up to loop under the right subclavian (the 4th arch). On the left, it stays hooked under the ductus arteriosus, which becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

**Venous system.** Three paired systems drain into the **sinus venosus**:
- **Vitelline veins** form the hepatic sinusoids, the portal vein, the superior mesenteric vein and the hepatic part of the IVC.
- **Umbilical veins**: the right one disappears. The left one carries oxygenated placental blood and bypasses the liver through the **ductus venosus**.
- **Cardinal veins**: the anterior cardinals, linked by a left-to-right anastomosis (the left brachiocephalic vein), form the SVC. The posterior, subcardinal and supracardinal veins together build the IVC and the azygos system.
levels.phd:
Arch-artery remodeling is a sequence of asymmetric survival and regression decisions laid on an initially symmetric plan. The endothelium of the arch arteries comes from pharyngeal mesoderm. Its smooth-muscle coat comes from **cardiac neural crest** (from the otic placode to somite 3), as shown in quail–chick chimera studies by Le Lièvre and Le Douarin and by Kirby's ablation work. Removing the cardiac crest in chick embryos causes persistent truncus arteriosus and arch-artery anomalies. This links arch patterning to outflow-tract septation.

The 4th arch artery is especially fragile. In **22q11.2 deletion syndrome**, losing one copy of **TBX1** disrupts how the pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm signal to the neural crest, through FGF8 and FGF10. Mouse *Tbx1* heterozygotes show a hypoplastic or missing 4th arch artery early in development. Many of them recover later, which matches the incomplete penetrance seen in patients. The clinical results include **interrupted aortic arch type B** (between the left carotid and left subclavian) and an aberrant right subclavian artery.

Left–right asymmetry is not decided inside the arches themselves. It comes from **Nodal–Pitx2** signaling inherited from gastrulation, together with haemodynamics. Yashiro and colleagues (Nature, 2007) showed that the rotation of the outflow tract, which Pitx2c drives in the second heart field, splits blood flow unequally between the 6th arches. Low flow on the right lowers PDGFR and VEGFR2 signaling, and that vessel then regresses. So flow-dependent pruning, not a fixed genetic map, carries out the asymmetry.

Regression of the right dorsal aorta is apoptotic and depends on flow. If the wrong segment regresses, the result is predictable using the **Edwards hypothetical double arch**. Persistence of both dorsal aortae gives a double aortic arch, a vascular ring. Abnormal regression of right arch 4 gives a retro-esophageal aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria).

On the venous side, the right-sided bias reflects the left sinus horn shrinking down to become the coronary sinus. Anastomoses then move blood to the right. The IVC is assembled from four segments: hepatic (vitelline), suprarenal (subcardinal), renal (the sub–supracardinal anastomosis) and infrarenal (supracardinal). Because it has so many parts, it is prone to variants such as a left or duplicated IVC.
levels.expert:
Clinically, arch and venous embryology mostly shows up as anomalies that are found by chance or that cause compression. Being able to reason from the Edwards double-arch model lets you predict any variant you see on imaging.

**Vascular rings.** A double aortic arch is the most common symptomatic ring. A right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and a left-sided ligamentum is second. Infants present with stridor, wheeze or difficulty swallowing. CT or MR angiography maps the dominant arch. Surgery divides the smaller (usually left) arch or the ligamentum, often through a left thoracotomy. A **Kommerell diverticulum** (a widened origin of the aberrant subclavian) may need resection because it can grow larger or dissect. Arteria lusoria can cause **dysphagia lusoria** in adults. It also matters for the right radial approach in catheterization, because the catheter course is altered.

**Genetic implications.** A right aortic arch, interrupted arch type B, or an aberrant subclavian together with conotruncal disease should prompt 22q11.2 testing. A right arch is common in tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus. Interrupted arch type A, by contrast, is less strongly linked to 22q11.2.

**Venous variants with procedural impact:**
- A **persistent left SVC** usually drains into the coronary sinus. It can complicate pacemaker leads, central lines and the delivery of retrograde cardioplegia. Its presence is suggested by a dilated coronary sinus on echocardiography.
- An **interrupted IVC with azygos continuation** is associated with left isomerism (heterotaxy). It changes access routes for catheter interventions.
- A **left or duplicated IVC** matters for filter placement and retroperitoneal surgery.
- A **retroaortic or circumaortic left renal vein** is relevant to donor nephrectomy.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Persistent embryonic carotid–basilar connections, such as the **persistent trigeminal artery**, are relevant before skull-base or endovascular procedures. Bovine arch configurations (shared origin of the brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid) affect catheter navigation during thrombectomy.

**Open questions.** Researchers are still working out how blood-flow sensing (shear-responsive KLF2 and endothelial cilia) works together with TBX1-dependent signaling to decide which arch segments survive. Light-sheet imaging and single-cell mapping of second-heart-field and neural crest lineages are now addressing the variable penetrance seen in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

keyPoints: Pharyngeal arch arteries 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 link the aortic sac to paired dorsal aortae
Arch 3 forms the carotids; left 4 forms the aortic arch; right 4 forms the proximal right subclavian
Arch 6 forms the pulmonary arteries and, on the left, the ductus arteriosus
Recurrent laryngeal nerve asymmetry follows asymmetric arch regression
Vitelline, umbilical and cardinal veins remodel rightward to form the portal system, SVC and IVC
Cardiac neural crest and TBX1 defects cause arch anomalies such as interrupted arch type B

test.q: Which arch artery gives rise to the common carotid arteries?
test.explain: The 3rd arch arteries form the common carotids and the proximal internal carotids. The external carotid sprouts from them.

test.q: The left 4th arch artery contributes to which adult vessel?
test.explain: The left 4th arch forms the segment of the aortic arch between the left common carotid and the left subclavian arteries.

test.q: What does the right 4th arch artery become?
test.explain: The right 4th arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery. The distal part comes from the 7th intersegmental artery.

test.q: Why does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop into the chest?
choices: It hooks under the left subclavian
It hooks under the ductus arteriosus
It wraps around the left SVC
test.explain: The left distal 6th arch persists as the ductus arteriosus (later the ligamentum), so the nerve stays hooked under it, low in the chest.

test.q: Which vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta in the fetus?
test.explain: The right umbilical vein regresses, so the persisting left umbilical vein brings placental blood to the fetus.

test.q: The ductus venosus allows blood to bypass which organ?
test.explain: The ductus venosus shunts umbilical blood past the liver to the IVC. The ductus arteriosus is the one that bypasses the lungs.

test.q: The vitelline veins mainly give rise to:
test.explain: Vitelline veins form the hepatic sinusoids, portal vein, superior mesenteric vein and the hepatic part of the IVC.

test.q: Below roughly T4, the two dorsal aortae:
test.explain: The paired dorsal aortae fuse caudally into a single descending aorta.

test.q: The left brachiocephalic vein forms from:
choices: A segment of the left umbilical vein
A remnant of the left supracardinal vein
A segment of the left vitelline vein
test.explain: An anastomosis between the anterior cardinal veins shunts blood rightward and becomes the left brachiocephalic vein.

test.q: The distal left 6th arch artery becomes the ductus ___.
test.explain: The ductus arteriosus lets fetal blood bypass the lungs. It later closes to form the ligamentum arteriosum.

test.q: Which numbered pair of arch arteries never forms or disappears almost immediately?
test.explain: The 5th pair is absent or transient, so the numbering runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.

test.q: The anterior cardinal veins help form the superior vena ___.
test.explain: The right anterior cardinal vein and the common cardinal vein form the SVC.

kidTest.q: What does the big aorta do?
choices: Carries blood away from the heart
kidTest.explain: The aorta is the main road for blood leaving the heart.

kidTest.q: How do a baby's early blood pipes look?
choices: Pipes on just the left side
kidTest.explain: They start in matching left and right pairs, like a ladder.

kidTest.q: What happens to pipes the body does not need?
kidTest.explain: Like closed roads, unneeded pipes shrink and disappear.

kidTest.q: To which side is most vein blood sent later on?
kidTest.explain: Veins move their blood to the right side so it can flow back into the heart.

kidTest.q: The main road for blood leaving the heart is the a _ _ _ _ a.
kidTest.explain: The aorta is the body's biggest artery.

advancedTest.q: An infant with 22q11.2 deletion has interrupted aortic arch type B. Which developmental failure best explains it?
choices: Persistence of the right 6th arch artery distal part
Defective left 4th arch artery from TBX1-related signaling
Failure of the anterior cardinal anastomosis to form
Excess regression of the right dorsal aorta segment
advancedTest.explain: Type B interruption lies between the left carotid and left subclavian, the segment built by the left 4th arch. TBX1 loss impairs 4th arch formation.

advancedTest.q: In the Yashiro model, why does the right 6th arch regress?
choices: Right arch endothelium carries a KLF2 gene deletion
Right-sided crest cells are absent from the start
Outflow rotation lowers right-sided flow and growth signaling
Nodal is expressed directly inside the right arch
advancedTest.explain: Pitx2c-driven outflow rotation splits flow unequally. Reduced right-sided flow lowers PDGFR/VEGFR2 signaling and the vessel is pruned.

advancedTest.q: A pacemaker lead passed from the left arm enters a dilated coronary sinus. What is the likeliest explanation?
advancedTest.explain: A persistent left SVC usually drains into the coronary sinus, dilating it and diverting leads from the left side.

advancedTest.q: If the right dorsal aorta fails to regress, the most likely result is:
choices: A double aortic arch forming a ring
An interrupted aortic arch type A
A left IVC with hemiazygos flow
advancedTest.explain: Persistence of both dorsal aortic segments preserves both arches of the Edwards model, encircling the trachea and esophagus.

lessons.title: Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth

levels.kid:
Before you were born, you lived in water inside your mom. You could not breathe air yet, so your lungs were not working. Instead, your mom's blood brought you oxygen through a special cord called the **umbilical cord**.

Your heart had clever shortcuts, like secret doors and side tunnels. They let blood skip the sleepy lungs and go straight to your body.

Then, at birth, something amazing happened. You took your first big breath! Your lungs filled with air like balloons. The secret door in your heart swung shut, and the side tunnel squeezed closed over the next few days. Now your blood goes to your lungs to pick up oxygen all by itself.
levels.hs:
A fetus cannot get oxygen from its lungs, because they are filled with fluid. Oxygen and nutrients come from the mother through the **placenta**, and the fetal circulation is built to send that blood around the lungs.

Key pathway:
- Oxygen-rich blood leaves the placenta in the **umbilical vein**.
- Much of it bypasses the liver through the **ductus venosus** and enters the inferior vena cava.
- In the right atrium, much of this blood crosses an opening called the **foramen ovale** into the left atrium, then goes to the left ventricle and out to the brain and heart.
- Blood pumped by the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery mostly crosses the **ductus arteriosus** into the aorta, skipping the lungs.
- Two **umbilical arteries** carry oxygen-poor blood back to the placenta.

Three shunts (ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus) are the stars of the show.

At birth the baby breathes. The lungs expand, the blood vessels in the lungs relax, and much more blood flows through them. Pressure in the left atrium rises above the right, pushing a flap shut over the foramen ovale. Rising oxygen levels make the ductus arteriosus constrict. Clamping the cord removes the placenta.

Example: if the ductus arteriosus stays open, called **patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)**, the baby may develop a heart murmur. PDA is especially common in premature babies.
levels.college:
Fetal circulation runs **in parallel** rather than in series: both ventricles pump into the systemic circulation, and the placenta, not the lungs, is the gas exchanger. Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high and systemic vascular resistance is low, largely because of the low-resistance placental bed.

**Path of oxygenated blood** (umbilical vein saturation roughly 80%):
- Umbilical vein → ductus venosus (bypassing hepatic sinusoids) → IVC.
- In the right atrium, the **crista dividens** and the valve of the IVC (Eustachian valve) direct this streaming blood across the **foramen ovale** to the left atrium.
- Left ventricle → ascending aorta, so the coronaries and brain receive the best-oxygenated blood.

**Path of deoxygenated blood**: SVC blood is directed mostly through the tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk. Because PVR is high, only about 10-15% of combined output reaches the lungs. The rest crosses the **ductus arteriosus** into the descending aorta, distal to the head vessels. The two umbilical arteries, branches of the internal iliacs, return blood to the placenta.

**Ductal patency** is actively maintained by low fetal oxygen tension and by circulating **prostaglandin E2**, made by the placenta and the ductus itself.

**Transition at birth:**
- Lung aeration, rising alveolar O2 and nitric oxide release cause a sharp fall in PVR, so pulmonary blood flow rises dramatically.
- Cord clamping removes the placenta, raising systemic resistance.
- Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure, which presses the **septum primum** against the septum secundum and functionally closes the foramen ovale.
- Higher O2 and falling PGE2 constrict the ductus arteriosus, functionally within about 1-3 days.

**Adult remnants:**
- Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres hepatis.
- Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum.
- Foramen ovale → fossa ovalis.
- Ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum.
- Distal umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments.
levels.phd:
The fetal circulation is best described quantitatively in terms of **combined ventricular output (CVO)**, since the two ventricles work in parallel. Classic chronically instrumented fetal lamb studies by Rudolph and Heymann, using radionuclide microspheres, established the textbook distribution. The right ventricle ejects roughly two-thirds of CVO in sheep, with somewhat less right dominance in humans by MRI and Doppler. Pulmonary flow is low: about 8% in lambs and higher in human fetuses near term, around 13-25% in MRI studies (Prsa, Seed and colleagues).

**Preferential streaming** is the key concept. Ductus venosus blood has high velocity and kinetic energy, and the crista dividens directs it through the foramen ovale. This delivers blood with an O2 saturation of about 65% to the left heart, versus about 55% in the right ventricle. Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, which shifts its O2 dissociation curve to the left (P50 about 19 vs 27 mmHg). This allows high saturation at a low PO2.

**Ductus arteriosus biology**: patency depends on PGE2 acting on **EP4 receptors** to raise cAMP, together with a low-O2 environment. Constriction at birth involves O2 sensing by mitochondria in ductal smooth muscle. Rising PO2 increases mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, which inhibits voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels. The membrane depolarizes, L-type Ca2+ channels open, and the muscle contracts; Rho-kinase signaling helps sustain the contraction. Placental loss and pulmonary metabolism of PGE2 remove the dilator.

Anatomical closure follows over weeks. Endothelial and smooth-muscle proliferation, neointimal cushion formation and fibrosis convert the ductus into the ligamentum arteriosum.

**PVR fall**: ventilation alone, oxygenation, and vasodilators all contribute. Shear stress and O2 increase eNOS-derived NO and prostacyclin (PGI2), while endothelin-1 tone falls. Classic experiments by Dawes and colleagues separated the effect of ventilation without oxygen from the effect of oxygenation. PVR falls by roughly 80-90% within minutes, then continues to decline over weeks as the medial smooth muscle remodels.

Cord-clamping timing matters physiologically. Studies by Hooper's group in lambs showed that **physiological-based cord clamping**, meaning clamping after ventilation begins, avoids an abrupt fall in preload and cardiac output.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the transition is the moment when ductal-dependent and shunt-dependent lesions declare themselves, so expect a heavily tested neonatal topic.

**Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)**: PVR fails to fall, so right-to-left shunting continues across the ductus and foramen ovale. The hallmark is **differential cyanosis**: pre-ductal (right hand) saturation exceeds post-ductal (foot) saturation. This explains the logic of **pulse oximetry screening** at 24 hours or more, comparing right hand with foot. That screening also detects critical congenital heart disease. Risk factors include meconium aspiration, sepsis and congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Management includes oxygen, ventilation, **inhaled nitric oxide** and, in refractory cases, ECMO. Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure has been associated with a small increase in PPHN risk, though the absolute risk remains low.

**Ductal pharmacology**, conceptually with no doses:
- **Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil)** keeps the ductus open in ductal-dependent lesions until surgery. Examples include hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical coarctation, pulmonary atresia, and transposition of the great arteries, where mixing is needed. Apnea is a key adverse effect.
- **COX inhibitors** (indomethacin, ibuprofen) and **acetaminophen**, which acts on the peroxidase site of prostaglandin H synthase, are used to close a hemodynamically significant PDA in preterm infants. Whether treating PDA improves long-term outcomes is still debated; recent trials (e.g., BeNeDuctus) support expectant management in many cases.
- **Maternal NSAIDs** in the third trimester can cause premature fetal ductal constriction. This is why regulators advise avoiding them, generally from about 20 weeks onward because of fetal renal and amniotic-fluid effects as well.

**Patent foramen ovale (PFO)**: anatomical fusion fails in roughly 25% of adults. PFO is linked to paradoxical embolism and cryptogenic stroke, which is relevant to neurology. Trials such as CLOSE, RESPECT and REDUCE showed that device closure benefits selected younger patients, guided by the RoPE score.

**Delayed cord clamping**, at about 30-60 seconds or more, improves iron stores in term infants and reduces mortality in preterm infants (meta-analyses by Fogarty and colleagues). It is now standard.

Open questions include ductal mechanobiology, the best timing for ventilation-based clamping, and fetal MRI-based oximetry for predicting brain growth in congenital heart disease.

keyPoints: The placenta, not the lungs, oxygenates fetal blood
Three shunts: ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus
Streaming sends the best-oxygenated blood to the heart and brain
At birth, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and left atrial pressure rises
Oxygen and falling PGE2 close the ductus arteriosus
PGE1 keeps the ductus open; COX inhibitors help close it

test.q: Which vessel carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus?
test.explain: The umbilical vein brings oxygenated blood from the placenta. The two umbilical arteries return oxygen-poor blood to it.

test.q: Which shunt lets placental blood bypass the liver?
test.explain: The ductus venosus carries umbilical venous blood directly into the inferior vena cava, around the liver sinusoids.

test.q: The ductus arteriosus connects which two vessels?
test.explain: It sends right ventricular output from the pulmonary trunk into the descending aorta, so that blood skips the lungs.

test.q: Why does little blood flow to the fetal lungs?
choices: The lungs lack any blood vessels
test.explain: Fluid-filled lungs and constricted pulmonary vessels give high resistance, so blood takes the shunts instead.

test.q: What closes the foramen ovale at birth?
test.explain: Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure. This pushes the septum primum against the septum secundum.

test.q: Which substance helps keep the fetal ductus arteriosus open?
test.explain: PGE2 from the placenta and the ductus, together with low oxygen, maintains patency. Rising O2 and falling PGE2 close it.

test.q: The adult remnant of the ductus arteriosus is the:
test.explain: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The ligamentum venosum comes from the ductus venosus.

test.q: Which drug class is used to help close a PDA in preterm infants?
test.explain: COX inhibitors such as indomethacin and ibuprofen reduce prostaglandin production. PGE1 does the opposite and keeps the ductus open.

test.q: Fetal hemoglobin helps oxygen uptake because it:
test.explain: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, which shifts its curve left and gives it higher oxygen affinity at a low PO2.

test.q: Blood crosses from the right atrium to the left atrium through the foramen ___.
test.explain: The foramen ovale is the interatrial shunt; it later becomes the fossa ovalis.

test.q: What abbreviation describes a ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth?
test.explain: PDA stands for patent ductus arteriosus. It is common in premature babies.

test.q: The adult remnant of the ductus venosus is the ligamentum ___.
test.explain: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum on the liver.

kidTest.q: How does a baby get oxygen before it is born?
choices: From its mom through a cord
kidTest.explain: The umbilical cord brings oxygen from mom's blood.

kidTest.q: Why does blood skip the baby's lungs before birth?
choices: The lungs are too big to use
The lungs are not working yet
The heart is too small to reach
kidTest.explain: The lungs are full of fluid until the first breath.

kidTest.q: What happens to the lungs at the first breath?
kidTest.explain: Air fills the lungs like balloons.

kidTest.q: What happens to the secret door in the heart after birth?
kidTest.explain: The door closes so blood goes to the lungs.

kidTest.q: The baby's lifeline to mom is the umbilical c _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The umbilical cord carries blood between baby and mom.

advancedTest.q: A newborn has a right-hand saturation clearly higher than the foot saturation. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Left-to-right shunting across a large atrial septal opening
High fetal hemoglobin affinity limiting oxygen delivery to tissues
Right-to-left ductal shunting from high pulmonary resistance
Early functional closure of the ductus venosus after birth
advancedTest.explain: Differential cyanosis means deoxygenated blood is entering the aorta below the head vessels, through the ductus, as in PPHN. An atrial shunt would not lower the foot reading selectively.

advancedTest.q: In the ductus, rising PO2 at birth triggers constriction through which sequence?
choices: Higher cAMP from EP4 signaling, then smooth muscle relaxation
More nitric oxide from eNOS, then a rise in cGMP within muscle
Lower endothelin-1 tone, then opening of potassium channels
More mitochondrial ROS, Kv inhibition, depolarization, Ca2+ entry
advancedTest.explain: The O2 sensor raises ROS, which inhibits Kv channels. The membrane depolarizes and L-type Ca2+ channels open. EP4-cAMP signaling is a dilator pathway.

advancedTest.q: Why do the coronaries and brain receive the best-oxygenated fetal blood?
choices: High-velocity ductus venosus flow streams across the foramen ovale
The right ventricle pumps directly into the ascending aorta
The ductus arteriosus joins the aorta before the head vessels
Superior vena cava blood is the richest in oxygen before birth
advancedTest.explain: Preferential streaming, guided by the crista dividens, sends umbilical blood to the left heart and ascending aorta. The ductus joins distal to the head vessels.

advancedTest.q: A neonate with critical coarctation depends on systemic flow through the ductus. The most logical initial therapy is:
choices: High inspired oxygen to speed ductal constriction
Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
Acetaminophen to inhibit prostaglandin H synthase
advancedTest.explain: Ductal-dependent lesions need the ductus kept open. PGE1 does this. COX inhibitors, acetaminophen and high oxygen would all promote closure.
